title: Celsus sets Moses against Jesus
source_text: Ἑξῆς δὲ τούτοις τοιαῦτά φησιν ὁ Κέλσος· ἐκεῖνο δ᾿ οὐκ ἐνθυμηθήσονται πάλιν; εἰ προεῖπον οἱ τοῦ Ἰουδαίων θεοῦ προφῆται τοῦτον ἐκείνου παῖδα ἐσόμενον, πῶς ἐκεῖνος μὲν διὰ Μωϋσέως νομοθετεῖ πλουτεῖν καὶ δυναστεύειν καὶ καταπιμπλάναι τὴν γῆν καὶ καταφονεύειν τοὺς πολεμίους ἡβηδὸν καὶ παγγενεὶ κτείνειν, ὅπερ καὶ αὐτὸς ἐν ὀφθαλμοῖς τῶν Ἰουδαίων, ὥς φησι Μωϋσῆς, ποιεῖ, καὶ πρὸς ταῦτα, ἂν μὴ πείθωνται, διαῤῥήδην αὐτοὺς τὰ τῶν πολεμίων δράσειν ἀπειλεῖ, ὁ δ᾿ υἱὸς ἄρα αὐτοῦ, ὁ „Ναζωραῖος“ ἄνθρωπος. ἀντινομοθετεῖ μηδὲ παριτητὸν εἶναι πρὸς τὸν πατέρα τῷ πλουτοῦντι ἢ φιλαρχιῶντι ἢ σοφίας ἢ δόξης ἀντιποιουμένῳ, δεῖν δὲ σίτων μὲν καὶ ταμείου μὴ μᾶλλόν τι φροντίζειν ἢ „τοὺς κόρακας,“ ἐσθῆτος δὲ ἧττον ἢ „τὰ κρίνα,“ τῷ δ᾿ ἅπαξ τυπτήσαντι παρέχειν καὶ αὖθις τύπτειν; πότερον Μωϋσῆς ἢ Ἰησοῦς ψεύδεται; ἢ ὁ πατὴρ τοῦτον πέμπων ἐπελάθετο, τίνα Μω(??)σεῖ διετάξατο; ἢ καταγνοὺς τῶν ἰδίων νόμων μετέγνω καὶ τὸν ἄγγελον καὶ ἐπὶ τοῖς ἐναντίοις ἀποστέλλει; πέπονθε δὴ διὰ τούτων Κέλσος πρᾶγμα ὁ πάντ᾿ ἐπίστασθαι ἐπαγγελλόμενος ἰδιωτικώτατον, περὶ τοῦ νοῦ τῶν γραφῶν οἰηθεὶς πλέον τῶν κατὰ τὸ γράμμα λέξεων μηδένα λόγον εἶναι βαθύτερον ἐν τῷ νόμῳ καὶ τοῖς προφήταις· οὐχ ὁρῶν ὅτι οὐκ ἂν οὕτω προφανῶς ἀπιθάνως τὸν σωματικὸν ἐπηγγέλλετο πλοῦτον τοῖς ὀρθῶς βιώσασιν ὁ λόγος, δεικνυμένων δικαιοτάτων ἐν ἄκρᾳ πενίᾳ βεβιωκέναι. οἱ γοῦν προφῆται καὶ διὰ τὸ καθαρῶς βεβιωκέναι τὸ θεῖον πνεῦμα χωρήσαντες „περιῆλθον ἐν μηλωταῖς, ἐν αἰγείοις δέρμασιν, ὑστερούμενοι, θλιβόμενοι, κακουχούμενοι, ἐν ἐρημίαις πλανώμενοι καὶ ὄρεσι καὶ σπηλαίοις καὶ ταῖς ὀπαῖς τῆς γῆς“· „πολλαὶ“ γὰρ „αἱ θλίψεις τῶν δικαίων“ κατὰ τὸν ὑμνῳδόν. εἴπερ δὲ ἀνέγνω τὸν Μωϋσέως νόμον ὁ Κέλσος, εἰκὸς ὅτι τὸ „δανιεῖς ἔθνεσι πολλοῖς, σὺ δὲ οὐ δανιῇ,“ λεγόμενον πρὸς τὸν τηροῦντα τὸν νόμον, ᾠήθη τοιοῦτον εἶναι, ὥστ᾿ ἐν ἐπαγγελίᾳ λέγεσθαι τῷ δικαίῳ τοσοῦτον πλουτήσειν τὸν τυφλὸν πλοῦτον, ὥστε διὰ τὸ πλῆθος τῶν χρημάτων οὐ μόνον Ἰουδαίοις δανείζειν τὸν δίκαιον ἀλλ᾿ οὐδ᾿ ἄλλῳ ἑνὶ ἔθνει ἢ δευτέρῳ ἢ τρίτῳ ἀλλὰ πολλοῖς. πόσα οὖν ἂν ὁ δίκαιος ἐκέκτητο χρήματα, μισθὸν τῆς δικαιοσύνης αὐτὰ κατὰ τὸν νόμον λαβὼν, ἵνα δανιοῖ „πολλοῖς ἔθνεσιν“; ἀκόλουθον δ᾿ ἐστὶ τῇ τοιαύτῃ ἐκδοχῇ καὶ τὸ ὑπολαμβάνειν ὅτι οὐδέ ποτε ὁ δίκαιος δανείζεται, ἐπεὶ γέγραπται· „σὺ δὲ οὐ δανιῇ.“ ἆρ᾿ οὖν ἔμεινε τὸ ἔθνος τοσούτοις χρόνοις ἐν τῇ κατὰ Μωϋσέα θεοσεβείᾳ, προφανῶς βλέπον ψευδόμενον ὅσον ἐπὶ τῷ Κέλσῳ τὸν νομοθέτην; οὐδὲ γὰρ ἱστόρηταί τις τοσοῦτον πλουτήσας, ὡς δεδανεικέναι „ἔθνεσι πολλοῖς.“ ἀλλ᾿ οὐ πιθανὸν οὕτως αὐτοὺς διδασκομένους ἀκούειν τοῦ νόμου, ὡς Κέλσος ᾤετο, καὶ προφανῶς βλέποντας ψευδεῖς (τὰς) κατὰ τὸν νόμον ἐπαγγελίας ἀγωνίζεσθαι περὶ τοῦ νόμου. ἐὰν δὲ τὰς ἀναγεγραμμένας τις ἁμαρτίας τοῦ λαοῦ φέρῃ παράδειγμα τοῦ καταπεφρονηκέναι αὐτοὺς τοῦ νόμου, τάχα διὰ τὸ κατεγνωκέναι αὐτοὺς ὡς ψευδομένου, λεκτέον πρὸς αὐτὸν ὅτι ἀναγνωστέον καὶ τοὺς χρόνους, ἐν οἷς ὅλος ὁ λαὸς ἀναγέγραπται μετὰ τὸ πεποιηκέναι τὸ πονηρὸν ἐνώπιον κυρίου ἐπὶ τὸ βέλτιον καὶ τὴν κατὰ τὸν νόμον θεοσέβειαν μεταβεβληκέναι.
pass_a_gloss: Next to these Celsus says (φησιν) such things: will they not consider (ἐνθυμέομαι) that again? If the prophets (προφῆται) of the God of the Jews foretold (προεῖπον) this one to be going to be his child/son (παῖς), how does that one legislate (νομοθετέω) through Moses to be rich (πλουτέω) and to hold power (δυναστεύω) and to fill up (καταπίμπλημι) the earth and to slaughter (καταφονεύω) the enemies (πολέμιοι) to the last youth (ἡβηδόν) and to kill (κτείνω) them with the whole race (παγγενεί), which he himself also does in the eyes (ὀφθαλμοί) of the Jews, as Moses says, and in addition to this, if they do not obey (πείθομαι), expressly (διαρρήδην) threatens (ἀπειλέω) to do to them the things of the enemies; but his son then (ἄρα), the Nazarene (Ναζωραῖος) man, legislates against (ἀντινομοθετέω) [saying] there is no access (παριτητόν) to the Father for the rich or the power-loving (φιλαρχιάω) or one laying claim to (ἀντιποιέομαι) wisdom (σοφία) or glory (δόξα), and one must not care (φροντίζω) for food (σῖτα) and storehouse (ταμεῖον) more than the ravens (κόρακες), and for clothing (ἐσθής) less than the lilies (κρίνα), and to one who has struck (τύπτω) once to offer (παρέχω) [oneself] to strike again? Which lies (ψεύδομαι), Moses or Jesus? Or did the Father sending (πέμπω) this one forget (ἐπιλανθάνομαι) what he commanded (διατάσσω) Moses? Or, condemning (καταγιγνώσκω) his own laws (νόμοι), did he change his mind (μεταγιγνώσκω) and send (ἀποστέλλω) the messenger (ἄγγελος) also for the opposite things? || Through these Celsus, the one professing (ἐπαγγέλλομαι) to know (ἐπίσταμαι) all things, has suffered a most layman-like (ἰδιωτικώτατον) thing, thinking about the mind/sense (νοῦς) of the writings (γραφαί) that beyond the words by the letter (κατὰ τὸ γράμμα λέξεις) there is no deeper (βαθύτερος) account (λόγος) in the law and the prophets; not seeing that the word (ὁ λόγος) would not so plainly (προφανῶς) implausibly (ἀπιθάνως) promise bodily (σωματικός) wealth (πλοῦτος) to those who lived rightly (ὀρθῶς), the most just (δικαιότατοι) being shown to have lived in extreme poverty (ἄκρα πενία). The prophets at any rate, having made room for/received (χωρέω) the divine Spirit (θεῖον πνεῦμα) because of having lived purely (καθαρῶς), went about (περιέρχομαι) in sheepskins (μηλωταί), in goat skins (αἴγεια δέρματα), lacking (ὑστερέω), afflicted (θλίβω), ill-treated (κακουχέω), wandering (πλανάομαι) in deserts and mountains and caves and the holes (ὀπαί) of the earth; for many [are] the afflictions (θλίψεις) of the just according to the hymn-singer (ὑμνῳδός). If Celsus read the law of Moses, it is likely (εἰκός) that he thought the 'you will lend (δανείζω) to many nations (ἔθνη), but you will not borrow', said to the one keeping (τηρέω) the law, to be such that it is said in promise (ἐπαγγελία) to the just man that he will be rich with so much blind (τυφλός) wealth, that because of the mass (πλῆθος) of money (χρήματα) the just man lends not only to Jews but not to one other nation or second or third but to many. How much money then would the just man have acquired (κτάομαι), having received it as wage (μισθός) of righteousness (δικαιοσύνη) according to the law, so as to lend to many nations? Following (ἀκόλουθον) from such an interpretation (ἐκδοχή) is also to suppose (ὑπολαμβάνω) that the just man never borrows, since it is written 'but you will not borrow'. Did then the nation remain (μένω) so many times in the god-reverence (θεοσέβεια) according to Moses, plainly seeing the lawgiver (νομοθέτης) lying, as far as Celsus is concerned (ὅσον ἐπὶ τῷ Κέλσῳ)? For no one is recorded (ἱστορέω) having become so rich as to have lent to many nations. But [it is] not plausible (πιθανόν) that they, being taught (διδάσκω) so to hear the law, as Celsus thought, and plainly seeing the promises according to the law false, would contend (ἀγωνίζομαι) for the law. If someone brings (φέρω) the recorded (ἀναγράφω) sins (ἁμαρτίαι) of the people (λαός) as example (παράδειγμα) of their having despised (καταφρονέω) the law, perhaps through having condemned it as lying, it must be said to him that one must read also the times in which the whole people is recorded, after having done the evil (τὸ πονηρόν) before (ἐνώπιον) the Lord, to have changed (μεταβάλλω) to the better and to god-reverence according to the law.
pass_b_english: Next after this Celsus says something like the following: “Will they not consider this point again? If the prophets of the God of the Jews foretold that this man would be his Son, how is it that through Moses he lays down that they are to be rich and hold power and fill the earth and slaughter their enemies young and old and kill them along with their whole race, which he himself also does before the eyes of the Jews, as Moses says, and besides this threatens outright, if they do not obey, to treat them as he treats their enemies (Numbers 33:56); while his Son, then, the Nazarene man, lays down contrary laws: that the man who is rich or loves power or lays claim to wisdom or glory has no access to the Father (Matthew 19:24), that one must take no more thought for food and storehouse than ‘the ravens’ do (Luke 12:24), and less for clothing than ‘the lilies’ (Luke 12:27), and that to one who has struck once one must offer oneself to be struck again (Luke 6:29)? Which of them is lying, Moses or Jesus? Or did the Father, when he sent this man, forget what commands he had given to Moses? Or did he condemn his own laws and change his mind, and is he now sending his messenger with the opposite charge?”

In saying this, Celsus, who professes to know everything, has made the mistake of a complete layman. As to the meaning of the Scriptures, he has supposed that the law and the prophets hold no deeper sense beyond the words taken by the letter. He does not see that Scripture would not have promised bodily wealth to those who lived rightly in a way so plainly unconvincing, when the most righteous men are shown to have lived in extreme poverty. The prophets, at any rate, who received the divine Spirit because they lived purely, “went about in sheepskins and goatskins, in want, afflicted, ill-treated, wandering in deserts and mountains and caves and the holes of the earth” (Hebrews 11:37–38); for “many are the afflictions of the righteous” (Psalm 34:19), as the psalmist says.

If Celsus did read the law of Moses, he probably supposed that the words “You shall lend to many nations, but you shall not borrow” (Deuteronomy 15:6), spoken to the one who keeps the law, meant this: that the righteous man is told, by way of promise, that he will grow so rich in blind wealth that, because of the abundance of his money, he will lend not only to Jews, and not just to one other nation, or a second, or a third, but to many. How much money, then, would the righteous man have possessed, having received it as the wage of his righteousness according to the law, so that he could lend “to many nations”? It follows from such an interpretation that one must also suppose that the righteous man never borrows, since it is written: “But you shall not borrow.”

Did the nation, then, remain for so long a time in the worship of God according to Moses, while it plainly saw, so far as Celsus’s view goes, that the lawgiver was lying? For no one is recorded to have grown so rich that he lent “to many nations”. But it is not plausible that they would have fought for the law if they had been taught to understand it as Celsus thought, and plainly saw that the law’s promises were false. And if someone brings forward the recorded sins of the people as proof that they despised the law, perhaps because they had condemned it as lying, we must tell him that he should also read of the times in which the whole people is recorded, after doing evil before the Lord (Judges 2:11), to have turned to the better and to the worship of God according to the law.

choices.choice: Celsus’s speech runs from ‘Will they not consider’ to ‘the opposite charge’; Origen’s reply begins at πέπονθε. The source has an OCR glitch ‘Μω(??)σεῖ’ (dative of Moses), read as Μωϋσεῖ. τὸν ἄγγελον καὶ ἐπὶ τοῖς ἐναντίοις: the καί is rendered by ‘with the opposite charge’ (sent the messenger, this time for the opposite purpose); ἄγγελος taken as ‘messenger’ (Jesus as God’s envoy), not ‘angel’. παῖς (‘child, servant’) rendered ‘son’ because Celsus goes on to call him ὁ υἱὸς αὐτοῦ. Allusions inside Celsus’s words cited inline where the wording is clear: Numbers 33:56 (God will do to Israel what he planned to do to the Canaanites); Luke 12:24 (κόρακας and ταμεῖον are Luke’s words, not Matthew’s ‘birds’); Luke 12:27 (also Matthew 6:28); Luke 6:29 (τύπτοντι ... πάρεχε; also Matthew 5:39); Matthew 19:24 for the rich man’s exclusion (also Luke 18:25), loosely paraphrased by Celsus as ‘no access to the Father’. Uncited allusions: ‘before the eyes of the Jews, as Moses says’ (Deuteronomy 1:30; 4:34); ‘to fill the earth’ (perhaps Genesis 1:28 or the seed promises, e.g. Genesis 28:14); slaughter of enemies to the last (Deuteronomy 7:2; 20:16); loving power and wisdom (Origen in 7.23 traces these to Matthew 20:25–27 and 1 Corinthians 1:20). ‘Nazarene’ (Ναζωραῖος) is Celsus’s term, kept. ἡβηδόν (‘from youth up’, i.e. every age) rendered ‘young and old’, παγγενεί ‘along with their whole race’; the same words are quoted back in 7.22. ‘Son’ capitalised in Celsus’s speech to match ‘the Father’ there: he means the Son claimed for the God of the Jews. LXX renumbering: Psalm 33:20 LXX = Psalm 34:19 English. Deuteronomy 15:6 LXX contains both the lending clause (here) and the ruling clause (7.19, 7.21); Deuteronomy 28:12 repeats the lending clause. ‘Blind wealth’ (τυφλὸν πλοῦτον) anticipates the Platonic contrast made explicit in 7.21. ‘After doing evil before the Lord’ is the recurring formula of Judges (2:11; 3:7; 3:12 etc.), followed by repentance; cited at its first occurrence. ὁ λόγος in ‘Scripture would not ... have promised’ means the scriptural word, not the divine Word, so lowercase sense rendered ‘Scripture’. θεῖον πνεῦμα capitalised as the Holy Spirit.
ἡβηδόν ... παγγενεί: 'to the last youth ... with their whole race' -> 'young and old ... along with their whole race' (not idiomatic English before)
'that that God lays down laws through Moses to be rich' -> 'through Moses he lays down that they are to be rich' (stiff order, doubled 'that')
'his son' -> 'his Son' (matches 'the Father' in the same speech)
ἀποστέλλει is present: 'and send his messenger' -> 'and is he now sending his messenger'
'a most unlearned mistake' -> 'the mistake of a complete layman' (ἰδιωτικώτατον)
reordered 'He has supposed, about the meaning of the Scriptures' into natural English
προφανῶς ἀπιθάνως: 'so plainly and implausibly' -> 'in a way so plainly unconvincing'
'nor to one other nation' -> 'and not just to one other nation' (οὐ μόνον ... ἀλλ᾿ οὐδ᾿)
restored ἀλλ᾿ ('But it is not plausible') and smoothed 'taught to hear the law'
all citations checked: Numbers 33:56, Matthew 19:24, Luke 12:24, 12:27, 6:29, Hebrews 11:37-38, Psalm 34:19 (LXX 33:20), Deuteronomy 15:6, Judges 2:11
